items.title: @SakanaAILabs Nice! This ends up being a version of what some of us have called "target prop": every...
items.content:
@SakanaAILabs Nice! This ends up being a version of what some of us have called "target prop": every layer's input is a free latent variable that serves as a target for the previous layer.
As this paper points out, this can be derived from an "augmented Lagrangian"  formulation of backprop in which the constraints (input of layer k+1 = output of layer k) are turned into penalties (divergence between input of layer k+1 and output of layer k).

I've always hoped more people would pick up on this idea. I'm happy this is happening!
I must say though that target prop, in the end, optimizes the same criterion as backprop and does the same thing as backprop while evaluating the gradient in a different way, perhaps more biologically plausible.

My lab did some work on this idea in the context of "sparse auto-encoders" in the late 2000s.  It turns out when the code in an auto-encoder is regularized (e.g. with L1 to make it sparse) target prop seems more efficient than backprop. 
https://t.co/uVDmnmFnbQ

Introducing our most advanced Gemini Audio models yet 🗣

Gemini 3.8 Live and 3.8 Live Extended Think...
items.content:
Introducing our most advanced Gemini Audio models yet 🗣

Gemini 3.8 Live and 3.8 Live Extended Thinking let you speak, collaborate, and execute tasks seamlessly, meaning conversing with AI just got a lot more natural.

So, what’s the difference between these two models? Let’s break it down:

— Gemini 3.8 Live is built for scale, speed, and cost efficiency. It can handle mid-sentence interruptions, transitions across 97 languages on the fly, and understands visual context. Figure out how to fix a broken bike chain, or deal with a leaky pipe just by pointing your camera at the problem area in Search Live for step-by-step audio instructions.

— Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking goes one step further to bring increased intelligence to your most complex tasks. It reasons and speaks in parallel, even narrating its progress as it works. This lets it handle multi-step, behind-the-scenes projects, like planning an event, without ever losing the conversational flow.

Watch how Gemini 3.8 Live combines real-time video and voice inputs in Search Live to tackle hands-on DIY plumbing tasks step by step 👇

items.title: Google has released Gemini 3.8 Live, its new Speech to Speech model, with the Extended Thinking (Hig...
items.content:
Google has released Gemini 3.8 Live, its new Speech to Speech model, with the Extended Thinking (High) variant debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 82.6, and #1 on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 68.6%

Gemini 3.8 Live is @GoogleDeepMind's successor to Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, a Speech to Speech model that executes tools and API calls in the background while continuing the conversation. It comes in two variants: the standard Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, which supports configurable reasoning effort. We evaluated the standard model and the Extended Thinking variant at High reasoning effort through the Gemini Live API.

Key takeaways:
➤ Speech to Speech Index: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) debuts at #1 at 82.6, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 81.5, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 81.3 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live debuts at #5 at 76.0, with both variants up on Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High at 71.5 (+11.1 and +4.5 points). The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference and Arena Task Success Rate
➤ Speech Agent Arena: Gemini 3.8 Live ranks #2 in preference at Elo 1083, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live (1096) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1053, and #2 on Task Success Rate at 93.2%, behind Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 94.6%. Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) trails at Elo 990 with 89.1% task success
➤ Tau Voice: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) takes the top spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 68.6%, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 67.9%, GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% and Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 56.5% - up from 37.7% for Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live scores 30.1%
➤ Big Bench Audio: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) scores 97.7% on audio reasoning, ahead of Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 97.2% and behind Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus at 99.2%. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live scores 91.7%
➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 1.18 seconds for Gemini 3.8 Live and 1.35 seconds for Extended Thinking (High), both well ahead of Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High (2.99s) and in line with GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s and GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s, though behind Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 0.70s
➤ Cost: Gemini 3.8 Live costs $0.84 per hour of input audio, the cheapest model in the Index and roughly half the $1.75 of Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. Extended Thinking (High) costs $3.50 per hour - cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at $4.80 and GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~3.1x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75

See below for more detail ⬇️

Also, I am not saying that LLM-based AI tools are useless. They are very useful.
We all use them.

But, by themselves, they are not a path to human-level AI. 
Architectures that understand the real world are not LLMs. 
The architectural components that enable current LLM-based AI systems to interpret images, videos, and other real-world signals are not LLMs.

An basic idea in scaling RL: Can we allocate more compute to the harder problems?

items.content:
An basic idea in scaling RL: Can we allocate more compute to the harder problems? 

We did this: If your GRPO group has all wrong completions, sample more with probability P (~0.9) -- in search of more GRPO batches with nonzero gradient. It works!

Called "Never Give Up" https://t.co/bNPn6EQsiE

items.title: I was not expecting things to go this way, but I think MCPs are better than CLIs for most integratio...
items.content:
I was not expecting things to go this way, but I think MCPs are better than CLIs for most integrations.

items.title: Guys, these insane setups are fun and all, but they don't actually make you more productive. You jus...
items.content:
Guys, these insane setups are fun and all, but they don't actually make you more productive. You just end up spending more time building the system than actually doing real work.

All you need is one agent session that farms out to others and acts as a manager. If something's not working, just tell that to your main session and it'll adjust the overall approach.

If you're using the best models available, you shouldn't need anything more than this. This is coming from a guy who runs hundreds of agents a day, dozens at a time, with spikes in the hundreds at a time.

I'll be writing more about this soon.

every time we bring it up or do anything there, g...
items.content:
memory has been a hot topic for the past ~2 years

every time we bring it up or do anything there, gets ton of interest, but nothing sticks

few takes on why below:

- how to update and then use memory needs to be pretty tightly integrated with the harness. so its hard to build a standalone memory product

- the hardest part of memory is the logic of deciding what to remember. storing and even querying memory is not necessarily hard. the logic of deciding what to remember is often (a) application specific, (b) just prompting, which makes it hard to productize

- memory is not that useful in a general purpose agent, but more for when you are doing repeated tasks. more high usage ai agent are not just doing the same task repeatedly

- memory hasnt really proven to be useful for coding agents, and most agent things that take off happen first in coding agents

fal head of engineering @isidentical reveals how reinforcement learning turned H3 Max into a frontier video model that generates 5 seconds of video in under 3 seconds, down from nearly 2 minutes:

"It's probably the only frontier video model from a quality and output and adherence perspective that can generate videos in real time."

"We took this open source base MiniMax H3 video model, what we wanted to do was not just make it faster, but improve its quality ahead of anything else by implementing reinforcement learning for verifiable concepts like video editing and prompt adherence."

"We were able to get the model from 120 seconds for a 5-second video generation, almost 2 minutes, to under 3 seconds for a 5-second video generation. Almost double real time, while improving its quality ahead of the open source version and ahead of many frontier closed source models."
@fal

items.title:
"Everything AI has achieved so far is but a drop in the ocean."

That's page one of a 75-page paper ...
items.content:
"Everything AI has achieved so far is but a drop in the ocean."

That's page one of a 75-page paper called "The Last AI Built by Humans," from 30+ researchers at ByteDance, Tsinghua, Shanghai AI Lab and six other institutions.

The paper ranks AI self-improvement on five levels. At Level 1, humans still decide what gets fixed. By Level 5, the AI is rewriting the process that builds its own successor.

They also sorted 491 existing papers onto the ladder, and 75% landed at Level 1 or 2. Under 6% made it to Level 5.

Level 5 is what Western labs have been warning about. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind each list AI automating its own R&D as a risk in their safety frameworks.

items.content:
fal head of engineering @isidentical explains why they’ll never pre-train a model and why compute may be the real moat in AI:

"We are never going to pre-train a model. That is not in the cards for us. fal is a generative media cloud, and wherever we see gaps, we are okay to adjust and evolve our form to fit in there."

"Today the gaps are not in pre-training. There are multiple companies rushing to pre-train the best image and video models. There is a big gap in real-time video generation, which we think we cracked with H3 Max."

"I don't think anyone in the world has enough inference compute today. We have been very aggressive building and procuring compute, anywhere from building our own data centers to renting as many GPUs as possible."

"The moat is not the software that you build, not the training that you do, it's essentially your focus to be always one step ahead. As long as you're one step ahead, you're able to capture more value than anyone else."
@fal

items.title:
These moments resonated:
- Tolan's response latency drifted from two seconds to two and a half. That...
items.content:
These moments resonated:
- Tolan's response latency drifted from two seconds to two and a half. That half second tanked essentially every product metric, and users wrote in to say their companion had gotten slow.
- Plivo treats a spoken phone number as a typed field with a validator, not a transcript. Accuracy went from about 30 percent to the mid nineties with no fine tuning.
- Hamming AI monitors 10,000 production voice agents. The real error rate is nearer 10 percent, and adversarial testing breaks roughly one agent in five.
- EliseAI has a background agent make the slow tool call and drop the result into context, so the main model believes it made the call itself.
- Say mm hmm to a realtime voice model and it stops dead to apologize. On a real phone call, up to a fifth of the time both people are talking at once.

Voice playlist:
https://t.co/xx1VOTKCDQ

"If you look at today's frontier models in LLM land, they spend so much more compute on post-training and RL compared to the pre-training phase. A pre-trained base model is like a Swiss knife. Good for many purposes but not the best in individual domains."

"For image and video, there is a single aspect that's very verifiable, which is prompt adherence."

"We essentially spent hundreds of thousands of GPU hours just making sure we can improve the model's quality."

"How do we take it from a minute to a 3-second mark? That's a 20X improvement."

"Combination of kernels, post-training, RL, system optimizations, prompt expansion, safety logic, upscaling logic, we brought the latencies significantly down while preserving and improving the quality."
@fal

SITUATION EXPLAINED: SemiAnalysis asks where a robot's brain should live.

• The essay is "A Brain T...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: SemiAnalysis asks where a robot's brain should live.

• The essay is "A Brain Too Big to Carry", and the question is whether inference runs on the robot or in a data center
• On-device gives fast, reliable responses but hits hard limits on compute, memory, power, and cooling
• Off-device removes those limits but adds network latency, which matters far more when the system is moving through the physical world
• Boston Dynamics' Atlas splits the difference. Fast movement runs locally, higher-level planning happens in the cloud
• Cloud-heavy means very smart robots with centralized intelligence. On-device means a far more distributed world of autonomous machines

@sophiadew: "A lot of people building robots want all of the model to live inside the robot itself, so you always have sovereignty over being able to run, and don't have to depend on any network issues."

items.content:
Factory COO @francesca_lab reveals the 3 things every real enterprise software factory needs: model choice, sovereign deployment, and end-to-end automation.

"One, model-agnostic by design. You need to have the ability to flex between all of the models, frontier, open source, because they're good at different use cases."

"Two, sovereign deployment. We really want enterprises to own their own intelligence. It's important for us that we are not building that intelligence. We want to help our customers build that for themselves and own that."

"The last piece is end-to-end software development lifecycle, covering that entire cycle from an engineer having an idea all the way through maintaining that code in a production code base."
@FactoryAI

items.title: Fun pitch story from Siri cofounder Adam Cheyer. We met up at @johnkwerner’s conference at Google to...
items.content:
Fun pitch story from Siri cofounder Adam Cheyer. We met up at @johnkwerner’s conference at Google today. That is him on the right.

His cofounder, Dag Kittlaus would arrive to a fundraising meeting a few minutes early.

Would put a $100 bill on the table.

He would tell the VCs who arrived a little early, "Hey, I got a problem. I need to make a reservation near my hotel for Indian food tonight. Anybody who can do this in less than a few minutes gets $100." 

Back in 2009, OpenTable would be able to reserve a seat for you, Yelp would be able to tell you the reviews, and Google Maps would sort of be able to tell you where the place was, but it wasn't integrated. They would be fumbling around on their new iPhones, unable to do the job. 

Then he'd pull out Siri and just say, "Hey Siri, can you make a reservation at an Indian restaurant near the Hilton that has high ratings for 8 p.m. tonight?" And of course, Siri would do it just fine. From then on, he had them in the palm of his hand, and he'd talk about how AI would solve all these problems. 

Today, that story seems a little quaint because you can use Grok, or Meta's Muse, or any number of AIs to do such a thing. But back in 2009, only Siri did that. 

That is how you get people's attention at a fundraising meeting, a little stunt like that to get them to pay attention and stop being so resistant.

Siri was the first consumer app to use AI. Adam ran the largest AI team in the world before that at @SRI_Intl

items.title:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Elon wants US and Chinese AI labs to test each other's models before release.

...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Elon wants US and Chinese AI labs to test each other's models before release.

• His proposal: instead of labs picking their own evaluators, they run safety test harnesses on each other
• OpenAI tests SpaceXAI, SpaceXAI tests Anthropic, and so on, with Chinese labs joining the same system
• It's reciprocal rather than unilateral, which is his answer to the objection that if we slow down, China won't
• The unresolved problem is IP. Handing your weights to a competitor is a different proposition than handing them to METR

@sophiadew: "This makes way more sense than asking frontier labs to grade their own homework."

items.title: Nextdoor CEO @niravtolia predicts the companies that survive the AI transition will have 3 things in...
items.content:
Nextdoor CEO @niravtolia predicts the companies that survive the AI transition will have 3 things in common: distribution, proprietary content, and AI adoption.

"Today if you're not an AI-created company, you're at risk, and that goes for every company no matter how successful those companies are."

"The companies that will be able to make that transition from non-AI native to AI fluent, those are gonna be the ones that own their own distribution, that own their own content, and then they also have to adopt AI themselves."

"If you relied on Google for traffic, it's a very difficult landscape right now. The good news for Nextdoor is we never did rely on Google for traffic."

"If you don't own your own content, chances are it's already inside an LLM, and we would all rather go get it in that LLM versus going to 10 different sites like we used to."

"And then finally, you have to become AI fluent. So even if you have your own distribution, even if you own your own content, if you're not using AI, you're not giving consumers what they want."
@Nextdoor

items.title: Video has always been a one way pipe. You watch. It does not change for you without a loading screen...
items.content:
Video has always been a one way pipe. You watch. It does not change for you without a loading screen and a new file.

Flam spent years on the boring hard part. Patented compression that packs many variants into one small file so interactive content can switch in under 10ms while streaming as fast as normal video. They call those Flicks. Brands already run them in the placements they buy.

QED led a $40M Series B. That is proof serious money is betting on interactive content as infrastructure, not another ad unit.

items.content:
Nextdoor CEO @niravtolia argues AI can become one of the greatest forces for good without ever replacing the human experience of community:

"The recent narrative about AI creating a master race of robots that will make humans extinct, I think that kind of extreme doomerism is very damaging."

"Not because it makes people wanna put stops on the evolution of the technology, but because it creates a narrative not rooted in anything real."

"Anything experiential with other people, that idea of community, that's not something that can be proxied by machines. I am a techno-optimist. I think AI is gonna be one of the greatest forces for good the world has ever seen. But I do not believe it can proxy community."

"Community is when we get together with multiple other people. Those interactions are not me and machine. Those are me and other people, and the me becomes we."
@Nextdoor

Otis - Hurricane 

Can Frontier AI, AGI or ASI Ever Predict a Dynamically Evolving Weather System wi...
items.content:
Otis - Hurricane 

Can Frontier AI, AGI or ASI Ever Predict a Dynamically Evolving Weather System with 100% Accuracy?

Hurricane Otis was not proof that AI systems did not see anything, satellites saw nothing. It was proof that observing a physical system is not the same as knowing its complete initial state. The initial conditions are important. 

On October 23, 2023, Otis was still a tropical storm with sustained winds near 50 mph, and forecasts expected it to be near hurricane strength when it reached southern Mexico. Roughly a day later, Otis had explosively intensified into a Category 5 hurricane with winds near 165 mph before striking Acapulco. Every single state of the art AI system failed to predict. 

Even satellite estimates temporarily underestimated what was happening. When aircraft reconnaissance reached-Otis, the National Hurricane Center reported that its measured intensity was well above the satellite estimate.

Why couldn't Advanced AI weather systems or satellites simply see it coming?

Satellites provide extraordinarily valuable observations, but they do not continuously measure the exact multi-dimensional state of every atmospheric and oceanic variable everywhere.

Temperature. Pressure. Humidity. Wind velocity at every altitude. Ocean heat. Convection. Cloud microphysics. Vortex structure.

Forecasting systems must reconstruct an approximation of this enormously complex state from incomplete observations and then propagate that estimated state forward.

Research attempting to reproduce Hurricane Otis demonstrates the difficulty. Scientists varied initial conditions, atmospheric datasets, convection schemes, spatial resolution, time steps and atmosphere–ocean coupling. Some configurations improved its trajectory and landfall prediction.

Yet none reproduced Otis's observed intensity or extraordinary rapid intensification.

Otis was a dynamically evolving system.

A hurricane is not simply an object moving across a map.

It is an interacting nonlinear physical system.

The system continuously feeds back upon itself.

NASA's observations of Otis captured this transformation. As wind shear weakened, precipitation increasingly wrapped around the center, the storm became more symmetric, and its internal structure rapidly organized. Otis progressed from a strong tropical storm to Category 3, Category 4 and finally Category 5 within hours.

This is where chaos theory enters.

Chaos does not mean that weather has no physical law.

A chaotic system can be completely governed by deterministic equations while remaining fundamentally sensitive to its starting conditions.

Make an extremely small error in the initial state and, initially, two forecasts may appear almost identical.

Allow the nonlinear system to evolve. However, and that tiny difference can amplify until the two trajectories describe substantially different futures.

What about Frontier AI?

AI can make enormous improvement.

A future Frontier AI could assimilate vastly greater quantities of satellite, radar, aircraft, buoy, ocean and surface observations.

AGI — or even an  ASI — might push this much further.

Superintelligence does not automatically create information that was never measured.

Therefore, will AGI or ASI predict weather with 100% accuracy? The answer is no.

items.title: Mathematics for Computer Science by Lehman, Leighton, and Meyer (2015) is a textbook designed for un...
items.content:
Mathematics for Computer Science by Lehman, Leighton, and Meyer (2015) is a textbook designed for undergraduate students in computer science and related disciplines who require a rigorous foundation in discrete mathematics and formal reasoning.

The text assumes modest initial prerequisites, requiring only an informal familiarity with basic sets, functions, and standard high school mathematics, before developing the theoretical machinery needed to model and analyze computing systems.

The textbook centers on mathematical methods and discrete structures, defining clear boundaries around discrete rather than continuous mathematics, and treats formal proofs as an indispensable mechanism for verifying software and hardware correctness.

items.content_html:
Mathematics for Computer Science by Lehman, Leighton, and Meyer (2015) is a textbook designed for undergraduate students in computer science and related disciplines who require a rigorous foundation in discrete mathematics and formal reasoning.

The text assumes modest initial prerequisites, requiring only an informal familiarity with basic sets, functions, and standard high school mathematics, before developing the theoretical machinery needed to model and analyze computing systems.

The textbook centers on mathematical methods and discrete structures, defining clear boundaries around discrete rather than continuous mathematics, and treats formal proofs as an indispensable mechanism for verifying software and hardware correctness.

Read this book with an AI tutor on @ChapterPal: https://t.co/7ll6IjJPbX

(All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account.)

items.title: 🇪🇺 Great data and actually I think we should use this kinds of data to completely turn around Europe...
items.content:
🇪🇺 Great data and actually I think we should use this kinds of data to completely turn around Europe's immigration policy:

- We should have super easy inflow for immigrants from countries whose previous immigrants have shown low crime rates

You're from Japan? Just fly here and you can stay forever

- We should then almost completely ban any inflow from countries whose previous immigrants have shown high crime rates with instant deportations

You're on the top of that list? You're not coming in, sorry. We have to keep Europeans safe first!

Then you can add special exceptions for people in those worst rated countries for high quality talent, think AI engineers, neurosurgeons, high IQ people, with no crime records. But that process will take a little bit longer than just flying into Europe

Then every year you check the data and you adjust the policy based on last 5 or 10 years of criminal history of immigrants from those places

I think this is the most common sense policy and it'll make Europe much safer

items.content:
The Principles of Programming Languages book by Mike Grant, Zachary Palmer, Scott Smith (2002) is now in @ChapterPal's collection.

This textbook provides an introduction to the foundational principles and formal semantic structures of programming languages, aimed at advanced undergraduate and graduate computer science students.

Designed for readers with basic proficiency in OCaml, elementary knowledge of C, and general familiarity with object-oriented languages such as Java or C++, the text assumes mathematical maturity in discrete mathematics, formal logic, grammars, and algorithms. 

Rather than surveying existing production languages, the book concentrates on language definitions, formal models, and implementation techniques, analyzing features by building and extending miniature core languages within the call-by-value functional family known as F-flat.

Read this textbook with an AI tutor: https://t.co/lTt66gURDY

items.title: Thatch CEO @chrisellisdc says healthcare has the wrong incentives because your insurer doesn’t have ...
items.content:
Thatch CEO @chrisellisdc says healthcare has the wrong incentives because your insurer doesn’t have to win your business, your employer already chose it for you:

"The problem is there's no penalty for denying a claim. If you're working at a company that offers a health plan and your claim gets denied, who are you petitioning to? You don't get to change the insurance. It's decided for you by your employer."

"In a world where consumers choose and you have an experience, whether it's customer service, a claim denial, or another issue, if you have an experience that's really bad, you could just switch. You're no longer locked into a single carrier."

"It's that ability to switch and an ability for the consumer to express their preference in an open market that is what ultimately changes the shape of supply in that market."

"Our long-term vision is to reorder the incentives around making consumers happy. When people make consumers happy, carriers, pharma firms, everybody will make more money, and it will be a win-win for everyone."
@thatch_ai

items.title: Tesla doesn't wait for your feedback about a bug, it automatically updates its software based on its...
items.content:
Tesla doesn't wait for your feedback about a bug, it automatically updates its software based on its millions of cars.

Most B2B companies still run customer feedback the old way. Waiting for a support ticket, receiving an angry Slack message, or getting an email that’s sent after the decision's already made.

By the time a humans notice the pattern, it's already too late.

I like BuildBetter because it applies Tesla's logic to your customers instead of your cars. It reads every call, ticket, and message the second it lands, so the pattern surfaces before a single account has to complain.

Tesla figured out cars don't need a human to notice bugs. BuildBetter figured out your customers don't either.

items.content:
How does @Zoom get it done for me?

Not by hosting my 150+ CXO Spice episodes. That was never the hard part. The follow up was.

Guests thank you note. Quotes pulled for the promo. Show notes drafted. Action items for my editor. Every episode ended with an hour plus of admin nobody sees.

Now the meeting ends and the follow up is already waiting. The summary, the draft note to my guest, the tasks assigned with deadlines. I review, I tweak, I send. What used to take an hour now takes twenty minutes.

That's the difference between a tool that helps you talk and a tool that helps you finish.

@Zoom Gets it Done. It has always been for me.

Curious what "getting it done" looks like beyond my podcast?
